Neuroscience

Persistent activity and working memory

Networks of neurons in the prefrontal cortex hold sensory information for seconds after a stimulus disappears. When an object appears in your field of vision, some neurons keep firing even after you look away. This is called persistent activity.

The dominant theory is that these neurons are wired into recurrent loops, where activity reverberates and sustains itself. Working memory is more than remembering, though. It is the ability to manipulate information, compare inputs from different sources over time, and use them to make decisions.

Modelling

Modelling network dynamics

Experimental neuroscience only offers a restricted view of how the activity recorded in the brain emerges. Building on experimental results, researchers develop models of neuron networks to show how a network could sustain a stimulus-specific activity by itself.

Spiking neural networks are widely used for this. They replicate how neurons behave over time much more closely than perceptron-based networks. In my PhD, I tested such models by injecting their synaptic conductances into living neurons using a network clamp.

Modelling

Why brain-like networks are hard to train

Training recurrent spiking neural networks through time is extremely challenging because of their non-linear interactions. Many approaches bring deep-learning advances to SNNs through backpropagation through time.

Other approaches take inspiration from the brain itself, such as three-factor learning rules and the well-known spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP).

AI

Performant but energy-hungry AI

Deep neural networks and transformers succeed largely because their structure is simple, feedforward and differentiable, so it can easily be scaled up.

That power comes at an enormous energy cost. It is a stark contrast with the brain’s sparse, event-driven computation, which runs on roughly the power of a light bulb.

Read my article on ANNs vs SNNs →
AI

A tale of two architectures: neuromorphic computing

Nobody has yet found a learning algorithm that trains SNNs as efficiently as backpropagation trains ANNs. Meanwhile, hardware better suited to running SNNs has made progress.

Standard chips use the von Neumann architecture, which keeps memory and processing in separate units. Neuromorphic chips place memory and computation together, which saves the large amount of energy normally spent moving information between the two.
